voice.reference_text: 大家好，欢迎来到 AI 高频词。每一期，我们只讲清楚一个词：它解决什么问题，怎么理解它，以及它在现实里意味着什么。

items.text: On November 12th, twenty twenty-six, Nvidia filed a surprise notice with regulators.
Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company, was out as CEO and as a director, effective immediately.
He'd run Nvidia for thirty-three years, and the filing didn't say why he was leaving.
The stock opened down more than ten percent, and still closed down more than four.
Four days before the filing, he'd written to all his staff. One line read: "I was unfaithful to my wife."
He didn't say with whom. It looked like a private matter.
And yet within days, Nvidia's board, the US Congress, and China's Foreign Ministry were all weighing in.
So here's our take: the US-China tech war turned one CEO's private life into a national security issue.
That's not the same as saying he quit over national security. The company still hasn't said why he left.
Before we go on, let's separate what's confirmed from what's only been reported.
Here's what's on the record. Huang admitted, in writing, that he was unfaithful.
Nvidia's board opened an investigation, citing reports that foreign intelligence had targeted him.
But the board also said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised.
And then he resigned, with no reason given.
Now, two more claims. Both are New York Times reports citing anonymous sources, and neither is confirmed.
One says US intelligence suspected a businesswoman close to him of spying for China.
She's a former executive at a Singapore company, and that company is an Nvidia customer.
The other says he'd had another relationship, with an executive who reported to him. Nvidia declined to comment.
Now, the other side. China's Foreign Ministry calls the "Chinese spy" claims groundless smears.
Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs says it never investigated the businesswoman for espionage.
Singapore police did look into her personally, though, over suspected false declarations when the company bought servers.
This February, they said there wasn't enough evidence against her. And no one has been charged.
So was the affair in his letter with the businesswoman? He didn't say, and we don't know.
Either way, here's the real puzzle: why would someone close to a CEO set off this many alarms?
Because Nvidia sells AI chips, and whether the best ones can go to China is the front line of the tech war.
Nvidia's own annual report admits it's basically shut out of China's data center market.
And what Washington fears most is chips slipping into China through Southeast Asia.
That's where the Singapore company comes in. The evidence against her fell short, but police are still investigating the company itself.
US export control officials have inspected it too. The company denies any wrongdoing, and there's no conclusion yet.
So you've got the top chips, a customer suspected of rerouting them, and someone close to the CEO.
Put those three together, and a private matter ends up under a national security magnifying glass.
Now look at how everyone responded. They all pointed to the same thing.
The board cited reports that foreign intelligence had targeted him.
Three Republican committee chairmen asked him for a closed-door briefing, on national security grounds.
On the day he resigned, the head of the House China committee said Nvidia needs leaders who put national security first.
And that chairman urged Congress to move fast on export control laws.
Even China's Foreign Ministry made it about tech, telling the US to stop fabricating a "spy narrative" to justify a tech blockade.
So for all the shouting, both sides agree on one thing: this is about chips.
Now, inside Washington. On chip sales to China, lawmakers in both parties want to tighten, while the White House keeps loosening.
And Huang was on the White House's side, so when the scandal hit, both parties used it to demand answers.
Take the tightening side first. In October twenty twenty-five, the Senate voted seventy-seven to twenty for a provision limiting chip sales to China.
Then in March twenty twenty-six, one senator from each party jointly asked the Commerce Department to review Nvidia's export licenses.
Trump went the other way. In August twenty twenty-five, he said he'd clear a chip for China if Nvidia would "pay us as a country something."
And after the scandal broke, he called Huang "a very honorable man."
Democrats went after Trump, asking whether officials were told not to investigate because of Trump's ties to Huang.
Republicans went after the Commerce Department and pushed export control bills.
But don't draw that line too neatly. Senator Warren, a Democrat, is also backing a Republican's bill to tighten exports.
The one clean difference is this: Democrats name Trump. Republicans don't.
Speaking of the two parties, there's a popular take in Chinese commentary: that Huang was a casualty of America's partisan fight.
Hong Kong outlet HK01 says Hu Xijin, a well-known Chinese commentator, first claimed Democrats and the Washington establishment were targeting Huang to get at Trump.
A day later, he changed his tune: Huang was a political casualty of vicious two-party fighting.
So first he blamed the Democrats, then both parties.
So we checked. Before he resigned, the only lawmaker we found publicly calling for him to go was Republican Senator Kevin Cramer.
And Trump, a Republican president, backed him the whole way.
The top House Democrat did say resigning "was the right thing to do," but only after he'd already resigned.
There's no record of either party pushing him out.
Besides, the board had plenty of reasons of its own: his admission, the report of another relationship, and a shareholder lawsuit.
We'd say no one sacrificed him on purpose. He did get caught in other people's fight, but nothing shows that's why he left.
Not everyone buys this. The strongest pushback says national security is just noise, and he left over plain corporate governance.
He admitted infidelity, then a relationship with a subordinate was reported, and the board accepted his resignation that very day.
Any CEO could be gone over that. In twenty eighteen, Intel's CEO resigned over a relationship with an employee that broke company policy.
We agree with all of that, and we never said he left over national security. The direct cause may well be governance.
But we're asking a different question: how does one CEO's affair end up in front of Congress and China's Foreign Ministry?
Intel's case never did. And we think the difference isn't what he did. It's what his company sells.
Even if the spy reports turn out to be false, everyone's already treating this as a national security issue.
When the headlines fade, remember this: the more critical a company's product, the less private its leader's life gets.
Where his private life ends isn't up to him. What his company sells decides it.
Coming up on November 17th, Nvidia reports its first earnings without Jensen Huang.
There's no date yet for him to go before Congress, and none of the investigations has wrapped up.
That's where things stand as of November 14th. None of this is investment advice, and we'll keep following the story.
